claims.text: Structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by lattice distortion and atomic-scale mixing.
Lattice distortion influences resistance to elemental segregation.
Atomic-scale mixing influences resistance to elemental segregation.
Lattice distortion influences resistance to nanoparticle coarsening.
Atomic-scale mixing influences resistance to nanoparticle coarsening.
Thermal annealing between 773 and 1173 K, with and without noble-metal doping, is proposed as an intervention for catalytic-operation conditions.
Thermal annealing between 473 and 1923 K, with and without noble-metal doping, is proposed as an intervention for thermoelectric-use conditions.
Lattice distortion and atomic-scale mixing modify the energy barriers for elemental segregation.
Lattice distortion and atomic-scale mixing modify the energy barriers for nanoparticle coarsening.
Higher lattice distortion will improve structural and chemical stability under high-temperature service.
Greater atomic-scale mixing will improve structural and chemical stability under high-temperature service.
Nanoparticles with lower lattice distortion and atomic-scale mixing will be more prone to degradation.
The proposed boundary conditions are 473–1923 K, noble-metal content below 10 at.%, and particle sizes from 5 to 50 nm.
In-situ high-temperature X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy can monitor structure and composition during annealing.

contradictions.description: The intervention is thermal annealing with and without noble-metal doping, whereas the baseline is defined as having neither doping nor annealing. This conflates two factors and does not provide separate controls needed to isolate annealing from noble-metal doping.
The study concerns high-temperature service, but an unannealed baseline is not clearly exposed to an equivalent thermal history, making the intended comparison ambiguous.
